reporting-org.narrative: Siasa Place (SP) is a civic-tech youth-led non-governmental organization (NGO), established in 2015 that specializes in working with grassroots youth, in building institutional structures to support youth participation in politics and good governance. SP targets youth (men and women aged 18 to 35 years) and develops their skills in policy review, supporting the creation of youth-friendly platforms for public participation in decision-making processes, including the budget process and social accountability. SP works in 12 counties including Uasin Gishu, Kakamega, Busia, Kisumu, Homa Bay, Migori, Kericho, Nakuru, Nairobi, Kitui, Lamu, and Mombasa.

title.narrative: Strengthening the Power of Youth Voices Quarterly Progress Report: January 2025 - March 2025

description.narrative: The program implemented a wide array of interventions to enhance youth engagement in civic and governance processes, including Community Agenda Setting Forums in Busia, Homa Bay, Kericho, and Nairobi; a training session for youth civic and governance champions; and three Community Sports dialogues in Kitui, Lamu, and Busia. Additional activities included ongoing social media engagements, the Social Media Leadership Accountability Board, facilitation of the People Dialogue Festival (PDF) 2025 featuring the SDG Village, and Gumzo Mtaani held on the International Day of Zero Waste (March 29, 2025). Intergenerational Dialogues under the GDC Africa Forum also took place to equip youth with the tools to advocate for policy change. Collectively, these interventions reached 64,160 participants 1,521 offline (990 men, 531 women, and 27 persons with disabilities) and 62,639 online (57,704 reached and 4,935 engaged) and involved 18 government officials from both national and county levels, including area chiefs, ward and village administrators, and members of county assemblies. The forums created a platform for public awareness on the rights, feedback on civic and governance challenges affecting the youth and developing advocacy strategies to address the concerns. For the period, 33 civic and governance challenges affecting young people were identified and 7 addressed including the completion of seven stalled or new community projects and various other improvements that positively impacted local communities. The completed projects includes newly constructed classroom at Chesanga Primary - Kericho(Bureti), repair of Lake Primary School - Homabay, reconnection of water at Makongeni Sub County Hospital - Homabay, allocation of classroom to PP1 and PP2 learners at Ondati Primary School - Ndhiwa, murraming of Rapenda Bumacheke Road - Budalangi, restoration of electricity in Kanziko and Mwangala Market - Kitui, murraming of Maili Nne Road - Kericho (Chepseon). Implementation of agreed advocacy follow-ups and the use of social media for advocacy among county-based youth platforms remain relatively weak. Follow-up efforts are often slow, and most online accountability initiatives at the county level are led by individual champions rather than organized groups. In response, the program is providing consistent support to group leadership while working with both individual champions and youth groups to build collective capacity. To enhance sustainability, the program is also establishing a collaborative platform that brings together individual advocates and group administrators to facilitate knowledge sharing and joint learning ultimately strengthening group-based advocacy and fostering more resilient accountability structures. In the next quarter, the program will continue with institutional capacity strengthening of the county based youth organizations in the project counties to sustain the advocacy and influence service delivery for the purpose of realizing dignity of young people

title.narrative: Strengthening Duty Bearers' Accountability Through Community-Led Advocacy: Success Stories from Homabay, Busia, and Kericho Counties

description.narrative:
Across Kenya, local civil society organizations are demonstrating the power of community-led advocacy in rendering duty bearers accountable and scaling up service delivery at the county level. Three recent success stories from Homabay, Busia, and Kericho counties demonstrate how focused civic action can deliver tangible development outcomes.
In Ndhiwa, Homabay County, the Initiative for Awareness and Development (IAD) CBO successfully advocated for safer and more dignified learning conditions for young learners. Children in PP1 and PP2 at Ondati Primary School were learning under a tree, exposed to harsh weather conditions. IAD CBO intervened by directly engaging the school administration and mobilizing public attention using social media. As a result of this pressure, the senior classes were allocated a new classroom so that the younger students could be relocated to a good indoor learning environment. This victory not only improved learning conditions but also demonstrated how responsive education authorities can be if communities do make some noise about their concerns.
Similarly, in Budalangi, Busia County, the Isangalo Arts Group tackled the long-standing issue of poor infrastructure by agitating for the construction of the Bumacheke–Rapenda Road. By petitioning the ward administrator formally, the group managed to have the road—critical for local transportation and economic activities—constructed at last. The example illustrates the part played by educated and mobilized citizens' action in compelling infrastructural development via institutional channels.
In Kericho County, the Kericho Civic Champions mobilized the public to take action on the deplorable state of the ECDE classroom and sanitation facilities at Chesanga Primary School. Through hosting a public baraza involving local leaders, the group facilitated free discussion and demand for action. This led to the construction of a new ECDE classroom, affirming the benefits of participatory governance and citizens' oversight in education development.
These stories emphasize one important shift: when citizens engage constructively with local government institutions, duty bearers must react. Enhanced accountability is not a theoretical hope—it is an empirical outcome when civil society groups utilize strategic advocacy mechanisms such as petitions, media releases, and people's forums.
As these case studies demonstrate, the construction of a culture of accountability begins with empowering communities to speak up, organize, and demand their rights. These successes set a blueprint for other locations, showing that sustainable development is achievable when citizens and duty bearers interact in open and receptive partnership.
